mainTopic: Why the תורה lists fins as well as scales, and which finless water creatures are permitted
overview: This amud first finishes a list of permitted fish. It then quotes a משנה: every fish with קשקשת (scales) also has סנפיר (fins), but not the other way around. The גמרא asks why the תורה mentions fins at all if scales are enough. A פסוק about scale armor already defines קשקשת, so רבי אבהו answers that the extra word is there to make the תורה great and glorious. A ברייתא then explains why the תורה says both 'eat' and 'do not eat': a person who eats a non-kosher fish breaks both an עשה and a לא תעשה. The ברייתא also learns that tiny finless water creatures are permitted. They are allowed in vessels, and the words 'of all that are in the waters' allow them even in pits, ditches and caves. The גמרא then works through the פסוק using the rules of כלל ופרט and כלל ופרט וכלל. The amud ends with רבינא starting a rule from ארץ ישראל about two general statements next to each other, and that rule finishes on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the list of permitted fish
steps.stepSummary: The last few fish names in an earlier list are given, and they are declared מותר.
steps.simpleTranslation: The akunas, the afunas, the kesaftiyas, the akhsaftiyas and the atunas are permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a list of fish species that began before this line, and says these fish are מותר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These are names of specific kinds of fish. The line closes a list, so nothing new is being argued here. Right after it, the גמרא moves on to the signs of a kosher fish.

keyTerms.meaning: The name of one kind of fish (the first name in this line)
This one is, it is considered

phrases.english: The akunas and the afunas,
phrases.notes: This line finishes a list of fish names that began before this point.

phrases.english: the kesaftiyas, the akhsaftiyas and the atunas
– it is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes a list of fish that started before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The fish named here are permitted to eat.

steps.title: The משנה about fins and scales
steps.stepSummary: A משנה teaches that every fish with scales has fins, but not every fish with fins has scales. Kosher fish need both signs.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned elsewhere: any fish that has scales also has fins, but some fish have fins and no scales. A fish with scales and fins is a kosher fish. A fish with fins but no scales is a non-kosher fish.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a משנה from מסכת נדה about the two signs of a kosher fish. This sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gives a fact about nature: scales always come with fins, but fins do not always come with scales. So in practice, if you see scales, you already know the fish is kosher. That fact is what drives the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: There, in another place (here, another מסכת)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical rule: checking for scales alone is enough to know a fish is kosher.

phrases.english: We learned there:
phrases.notes: "There" means a משנה in מסכת נדה.

phrases.english: Any fish that has scales
has fins,
but there are fish that have fins
and do not have scales.

phrases.aramaic: יֵשׁ לוֹ קַשְׂקֶשֶׂת וְיֵשׁ לוֹ סְנַפִּיר
phrases.english: If it has scales and has fins
– it is a kosher fish;

phrases.aramaic: יֵשׁ לוֹ סְנַפִּיר וְאֵין לוֹ קַשְׂקֶשֶׂת
phrases.english: if it has fins and no scales
– it is a non-kosher fish.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the signs of a kosher fish.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Scales always come with fins. A fish with both is kosher, and a fish with fins only is not.

steps.title: Why does the תורה mention fins at all?
steps.stepSummary: Since scales alone tell us a fish is kosher, the גמרא asks why the תורה also wrote fins.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now, since we rely on scales, let the תורה write only "scales" and not write "fins"!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of the פסוק. If scales are enough, the word סנפיר seems extra.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה just said every fish with קשקשת has סנפיר. So the only sign we really need to check is קשקשת. A word in the תורה that adds nothing needs an explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: Now, since (opens an argument based on something already known)
The Merciful One, meaning the תורה

phrases.english: Now, since we rely on scales,
let the Merciful One write "scales"
phrases.notes: The פסוק that lists both signs is ויקרא 11:9.

phrases.english: and not write "fins"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the fact from the משנה to question the wording of the פסוק.
steps.kashyaTarget: The word סנפיר in the פסוק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If scales always come with fins, the word סנפיר adds nothing we need for the halacha.

steps.title: Without "fins," we might confuse scales with fins
steps.stepSummary: If the תורה wrote only קשקשת, we might have thought the word means fins and permitted non-kosher fish. Writing both words shows they are two different things.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the תורה had written "scales" and not "fins," I would have said: what is קשקשת? Fins. Then I would permit even a non-kosher fish. So the תורה wrote "fins and scales."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the word סנפיר is needed so we do not misunderstand what קשקשת means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With only one word, a reader might guess that קשקשת means fins. Then any fish with fins would seem kosher, even one without scales. Writing both words shows that קשקשת is something other than fins.

keyTerms.meaning: I would have thought (a mistaken first assumption)

steps.confusionAlert: The answer is not that fins are a second sign we must check. Scales are still enough. The word סנפיר is there only to show what קשקשת does NOT mean.

phrases.english: If the Merciful One had written "scales"
and had not written "fins,"
I would have said:
What is "kaskeset"? Fins,
and so even a non-kosher fish would be permitted.
So the Merciful One wrote "fins and scales."

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי כְּתַב רַחֲמָנָא קַשְׂקֶשֶׂת וְלָא כְּתַב סְנַפִּיר, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the extra word prevents a misreading
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With only one word, קשקשת might be read as fins, which would permit fish without scales.
steps.terutzMaskana: Writing both words shows קשקשת is not fins.

steps.title: A פסוק shows that קשקשת means armor-like covering
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know that קשקשת means a covering like clothing, and proves it from a פסוק describing a coat of scale armor.
steps.simpleTranslation: But now that the תורה wrote "fins and scales," how do we know that קשקשת is a kind of clothing? Because it is written: "And he was clad with a coat of scale armor."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק that shows what קשקשת means. This prepares a new challenge to the answer in step 4.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק uses the same word, קשקשים, for armor that someone wears. So the meaning of קשקשת can be learned from this פסוק: a covering like clothing, which is scales and not fins. The next step will use this to bring back the question.

phrases.english: But now that the Merciful One has written
"fins and scales,"
how do we know that "kaskeset" means clothing?
As it is written: "And he was clad with a coat of scale armor,"

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַשְׁתָּא דִּכְתַב רַחֲמָנָא סְנַפִּיר וְקַשְׂקֶשֶׂת, מִמַּאי דְּקַשְׂקֶשֶׂת לְבוּשָׁא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Looks again at step 4 by asking where the meaning of קשקשת really comes from.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What source tells us that קשקשת means scales, a covering like clothing?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק "ושריון קשקשים הוא לבוש" uses the word for worn armor.

steps.title: The question returns: why write fins?
steps.stepSummary: Since the פסוק already tells us קשקשת means scales, there is no risk of confusing it with fins. So the word סנפיר again seems extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: So let the תורה write only "scales" and not write "fins"!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings back its first question, because the answer in step 4 no longer seems to work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 said סנפיר was needed so we would not think קשקשת means fins. But step 5 showed that the פסוק about armor already teaches the meaning of קשקשת. So the worry from step 4 is gone, and the word סנפיר again seems to add nothing. The next step answers this.

phrases.english: So let the Merciful One write "scales"
and not write "fins"?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלִיכְתּוֹב רַחֲמָנָא קַשְׂקֶשֶׂת וְלָא לִיכְתּוֹב סְנַפִּיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the proof of step 5 to undo the answer of step 4 and bring back the question of step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 4, that סנפיר prevents misreading קשקשת
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק about armor already defines קשקשת, so there is no misreading to prevent, and סנפיר is extra again.

steps.title: The extra word makes the Torah greater
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו, backed by the school of רבי ישמעאל, answers that the תורה sometimes adds words that are not strictly needed, to make the תורה great and glorious.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said, and the school of רבי ישמעאל taught the same: the extra word is there because of the פסוק 'to make תורה great and glorious.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 6: why did the תורה write סנפיר if it is not needed? The answer is that the תורה adds extra words just to make itself bigger and more glorious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 6 every practical reason for writing סנפיר had fallen away. Instead of finding a new legal lesson, רבי אבהו says the word is there for its own sake. Having more תורה to learn is itself a good thing.

keyTerms.meaning: He will make the תורה great and glorious (ישעיהו 42:21)

steps.whatToRemember: Sometimes the answer to 'why is this word extra?' is not a new law. It can simply be that the תורה wanted to be greater and fuller.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't look for a hidden law in the word סנפיר here. The גמרא openly says the word is there only to make the תורה greater.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said,
and so the tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
"To make Torah great and glorious."
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 42:21. He means ה׳ added words to make the תורה bigger, even when they aren't strictly needed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ, וְכֵן תָּנָא דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 6 about why סנפיר is written.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the word as an addition with no new law, written to make the תורה greater
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every word must teach a practical law, so סנפיר should not be needed.
steps.terutzMaskana: סנפיר is written to make the תורה great and glorious.

steps.title: Why say both 'eat' and 'do not eat'?
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא points out that each half of the fish rule already implies the other half, so it asks why the תורה wrote both.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבנן taught: from 'eat what has signs' I would already know 'do not eat what lacks them,' and from 'do not eat what lacks them' I would already know 'eat what has them.' So why did the תורה write both?
steps.whatsHappening: A new ברייתא notices that the תורה gives the fish rule twice: once as permission and once as a ban. It asks why both are needed when each one implies the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The logic is simple. If only fish with signs may be eaten, then fish without signs may not, and the reverse is also true. So one of the two פסוקים looks extra.

keyTerms.meaning: From the implication, from what we understand on our own
I would understand, I could figure out
So why did it teach both of them?

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
From the implication of what is stated,
"Eat that which has [fins and scales],"

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹמֵעַ אֲנִי ״אַל תֹּאכַל אֶת שֶׁאֵין לוֹ״,
phrases.english: I would understand "Do not eat that which does not have them,"
and from the implication of what is stated,
"Do not eat that which does not have them,"
I would understand "Eat that which has them."
So why did it teach both of them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of seemingly extra words in the fish פסוקים with a new ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Each half implies the other, so writing both seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Two commands are broken
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא answers that the תורה wrote both so that someone who eats a non-kosher fish breaks both a positive command and a negative command.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason is so that he transgresses on it both a positive command and a negative command.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its own question. Both פסוקים are written so that eating a non-kosher fish counts as breaking two commands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'eat what has signs' wording becomes a positive command, an עשה. The 'do not eat' wording is a לא תעשה. So the repetition is not extra: it adds a second command to the same act.

phrases.english: To make one transgress on its account
with a positive command and a negative command.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the repetition adds an extra command
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The second פסוק is only a restatement.
steps.terutzMaskana: Eating non-kosher fish breaks both an עשה and a לא תעשה.

steps.title: Why say 'of all that are in the waters'?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks what the words 'You may eat of all that are in the waters' come to teach, since the rule about signs is already given.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'You may eat of all that are in the waters': what does the verse come to teach?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא points to another phrase in the פסוק that seems unneeded. It asks what the words 'of all that are in the waters' add. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק already says which fish may be eaten: those with fins and scales. So the opening words 'of all that are in the waters' look extra and must have their own lesson.

keyTerms.meaning: What does the verse come to teach? Why was it written?

phrases.english: "You may eat of all that are in the waters,"
what does the verse come to teach?

steps.triggerLanguage: ״תֹּאכְלוּ מִכֹּל אֲשֶׁר בַּמָּיִם״, מָה תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a different phrase in the same פסוק.
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase 'of all that are in the waters'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The rule of signs is already stated, so this phrase seems to add nothing.

steps.title: Permitted even in pits, ditches and caves
steps.stepSummary: Without this phrase, we might think tiny finless water creatures are permitted only in vessels. The phrase teaches they are permitted even in pits, ditches and caves.
steps.simpleTranslation: One might have thought: since the תורה permitted these creatures in an explicit way and also in an unspecified way, then just as the explicit permission covers only vessels, so does the unspecified one. From where do we include pits, ditches and caves, so a person may bend down and drink from them without holding back? The verse says 'You may eat of all that are in the waters.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers step 10. The phrase 'of all that are in the waters' teaches that tiny finless creatures in the water are permitted not only in a vessel but also in pits, ditches and caves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry was that the unspecified permission should be limited to match the explicit one, which covers vessels only. The extra phrase widens the permission to any standing water. So a person may drink from a pit even if tiny creatures are in it.

keyTerms.meaning: Pits, ditches and caves (places holding water)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not about fish with signs. It is about tiny water creatures with no fins or scales that may be swallowed along with the water.

phrases.english: For one might have thought:
since [the Torah] permitted explicitly
and permitted without specifying,
just as when it permitted explicitly
it permitted only in vessels,
so too, when it permitted without specifying,
it permitted only in vessels.
From where do we include
pits, ditches, and caves,
that one may bend down and drink from them
and need not hold back?
The verse says: "You may eat of all that are in the waters."

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁיָּכוֹל הוֹאִיל וְהִתִּיר בִּמְפוֹרָשׁ וְהִתִּיר בִּסְתָם
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the phrase widens a permission
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Tiny finless creatures are permitted only in vessels, to match the explicit permission.
steps.terutzMaskana: They are permitted even in pits, ditches and caves, so one may drink from them freely.

steps.title: Where did the Torah permit vessels?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where the תורה gave the explicit permission for creatures in vessels that the ברייתא mentioned.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where did the תורה permit them in vessels?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question about the ברייתא: where is the 'explicit' permission for vessels found? This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא assumed that a permission for vessels exists but did not say where it comes from. The גמרא wants to find its source in the פסוק.

phrases.english: Where did it permit them in vessels?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of an assumption made in step 11.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The פסוק that permits finless creatures found in vessels.

steps.title: Seas and rivers need signs, vessels do not
steps.stepSummary: The words 'in the seas and in the rivers' limit the need for signs to those places, so creatures in vessels are permitted even without signs.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'These you may eat of all that are in the waters' and so on. Only in the seas and rivers: if it has signs, eat it, and if it doesn't, don't. But in vessels, even if it has no signs, eat it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 12. The פסוק says signs are needed 'in the seas and in the rivers,' which implies that in vessels signs are not needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק could have said just 'in the waters.' By naming seas and rivers, it limits the rule of signs to those places. A vessel is outside that limit, so finless creatures in it are permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: In the seas and in the rivers
It has / it does not have (the signs)
But (here it shows what follows from the limit)

steps.whatToRemember: Signs are required for creatures in seas and rivers. Tiny finless creatures in vessels are permitted from the words 'seas and rivers,' and those in pits, ditches and caves are permitted from 'of all that are in the waters.'

phrases.english: As it is written:

phrases.aramaic: ״אֶת זֶה תֹּאכְלוּ מִכֹּל אֲשֶׁר בַּמָּיִם וְגוֹ׳״,
phrases.english: "These you may eat of all that are in the waters, etc."
phrases.notes: ויקרא 11:9. The 'etc.' continues: 'in the seas and in the rivers, them you may eat.'

phrases.english: It is in the seas and in the rivers
that when it has [signs], eat it;
when it does not have them, do not eat it;
but in vessels,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּלֵית לֵיהּ – אֱכוֹל.
phrases.english: even though it does not have them, eat it.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב: ״אֶת זֶה תֹּאכְלוּ מִכֹּל אֲשֶׁר בַּמָּיִם״
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The words 'in the seas and in the rivers' limit the need for signs to those places, so vessels are permitted.

steps.title: Maybe vessels are forbidden even with signs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the opposite reading: maybe in כלים you may not eat even a creature that has fins and scales.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say instead: in vessels, even if it has fins and scales, you may not eat it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reading from Step 13. Maybe 'in the seas and in the rivers' means only there are fish allowed at all, so in כלים even a fish with signs would be forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 13 read 'in the seas and in the rivers' as a limit on where signs are needed. This קשיא flips it: maybe it limits where eating is allowed. Then כלים would be stricter, not more lenient.

keyTerms.meaning: Say instead; maybe the reading is different
That it has (the signs of fins and scales)

phrases.english: Say instead: in vessels,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּאִית לֵיהּ לָא תֵּיכוֹל?
phrases.english: even though it has [the signs], you may not eat it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵימָא: בְּכֵלִים – אַף עַל גַּב דְּאִית לֵיהּ לָא תֵּיכוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading of 'in the seas and in the rivers' given in Step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 13 that creatures in כלים are permitted without signs.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The limiting words could just as easily limit where eating is allowed, which would make כלים forbidden even with signs.

steps.title: A second verse proves vessels are lenient
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the challenge. The פסוק about forbidden fish says 'in the seas and in the rivers', so only there is a creature without signs forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: That cannot be, because it is written: 'And all that have no fins and scales in the seas and in the rivers, of all that swarm in the waters.' In the seas and rivers, one without signs you may not eat. But in vessels, even without signs, eat it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 14 by bringing the פסוק that lists what is forbidden. It also says 'in the seas and in the rivers', and that proves כלים are the lenient case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The forbidding פסוק limits the ban on creatures without סנפיר וקשקשת to seas and rivers. So in כלים the ban does not apply, and the creature is permitted even without signs. This confirms the reading in Step 13 and rules out the reverse reading.

keyTerms.meaning: It cannot enter your mind; that idea is wrong
Fins and scales, the kosher signs of fish
Creatures that swarm in the water

steps.whatToRemember: Creatures found in כלים are permitted even without fins and scales, because the ban is limited to seas and rivers.

phrases.english: That cannot enter your mind, as it is written:
"And all that have no fins and scales
in the seas and in the rivers, of all that swarm in the waters" —

phrases.aramaic: בַּיַּמִּים וּבַנְּחָלִים דְּלֵית לֵיהּ לָא תֵּיכוֹל,
phrases.english: in the seas and in the rivers, one that does not have [signs] you may not eat;

phrases.aramaic: הָא בְּכֵלִים – אַף עַל גַּב דְּלֵית לֵיהּ אֱכוֹל.
phrases.english: but in vessels, even though it does not have [signs], eat it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 14 with a different פסוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings a second פסוק that settles which reading is correct.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe כלים are stricter, and even fish with signs found there are forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ban on creatures without signs applies only in seas and rivers, so creatures in כלים are permitted even without signs.

steps.title: A general rule and detail would already permit pits
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges why the ברייתא needed an extra phrase. It reads 'in the waters' as a כלל and 'in the seas and rivers' as a פרט, and a כלל ופרט would already exclude channels and trenches.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say: 'in the waters' is a general statement, and 'in the seas and in the rivers' is a detail. With a general statement followed by a detail, the general statement includes only what is in the detail. So seas and rivers, yes; channels and trenches, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to Step 11 and asks why we need 'of all that are in the waters' to permit pits, ditches and caves. A basic rule of reading the תורה already seems to give that result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the rule of כלל ופרט, the general word is limited to the detail. So the need for signs would apply only in seas and rivers. Water in channels, trenches and similar places would then be permitted without any extra phrase, which makes the phrase from Step 11 look unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: A general statement in a פסוק
A specific detail in a פסוק
A general statement followed by a detail; the rule includes only the detail

steps.confusionAlert: Under this reading the detail limits where signs are NEEDED. So channels and trenches being excluded means they are permitted without signs, not forbidden.

phrases.english: But say: "In the waters" — is a general statement,
phrases.notes: From ויקרא 11:9, 'whatever has fins and scales in the waters'.

phrases.english: "In the seas and in the rivers" — is a detail;

phrases.aramaic: כְּלָל וּפְרָט – אֵין בַּכְּלָל אֶלָּא מַה שֶּׁבַּפְּרָט;
phrases.english: a general statement and a detail — the general statement includes only what is in the detail;
seas and rivers — yes [signs are needed],
channels and trenches — no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ברייתא's answer in Step 11 and challenges whether its extra phrase is needed.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's claim in Step 11 that 'of all that are in the waters' is needed to permit pits, ditches and caves.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A כלל ופרט in the same פסוק already limits the need for signs to seas and rivers, so the extra phrase would add nothing.

steps.title: The verse says 'in the waters' again
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'in the waters' appears a second time, so the פסוק is a כלל ופרט וכלל.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'In the waters' — the verse came back and made a general statement again.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 16. The word במים shows up twice, so this is not a simple כלל ופרט.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With two general statements and a detail, the rule becomes כלל ופרט וכלל. That rule includes everything similar to the detail, so pits, ditches and caves would also need signs. That is why the extra phrase from Step 11 is needed to permit them.

keyTerms.meaning: It came back and made a general statement again
General, detail, general; includes everything similar to the detail

phrases.english: "In the waters" — it came back and made a general statement.
phrases.notes: The word במים appears twice in ויקרא 11:9, so there are two general statements.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reads the structure of the פסוק as a כלל ופרט וכלל.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק is a simple כלל ופרט, so only seas and rivers need signs.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק is a כלל ופרט וכלל, which would make places like pits need signs. So the extra phrase is needed to permit them.

steps.title: The two general statements sit side by side
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that both general statements come before the detail and are right next to each other, so this is not a real כלל ופרט וכלל.
steps.simpleTranslation: But these are two general statements that are next to each other!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer in Step 17. Both mentions of במים come before 'in the seas and in the rivers', so there is no general statement after the detail.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A כלל ופרט וכלל needs a general statement, then a detail, then another general statement. Here both general statements come first and the detail comes last. So the second במים does not seem to close the pattern.

keyTerms.meaning: That are next to each other

phrases.english: These are two general statements
that are next to each other!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנֵי תְּרֵי כְּלָלֵי דִּסְמִיכִי לַהֲדָדֵי נִינְהוּ
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the פסוק is a כלל ופרט וכלל.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both general statements come before the detail, so the order does not fit a כלל ופרט וכלל.

steps.title: רבינא brings a rule from ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: רבינא begins to answer with a rule taught in ארץ ישראל about two general statements that sit next to each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: As they say in the West: wherever you find two general statements next to each other —
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא starts answering the objection of Step 18 with a rule from ארץ ישראל. The sentence is cut off here, and the rule finishes in the next part of the גמרא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here רבינא only sets up the case: two general statements placed side by side. What the rule says about such a case comes next. That ending will explain how this פסוק can still work like a כלל ופרט וכלל.

keyTerms.meaning: General statements placed next to each other

phrases.english: רבינא said: As they say in the West,
phrases.notes: 'The West' means ארץ ישראל, which is west of Bavel.

phrases.english: wherever you find
two general statements next to each other —

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the answer to the objection of Step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings a general rule of reading the תורה from ארץ ישראל. The rule is completed later.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Two general statements next to each other cannot form a כלל ופרט וכלל.
steps.terutzMaskana: Not finished yet. The rule about adjacent general statements is completed in the next lines.
